articles.author: Allison Aubrey
articles.description: As part of her new podcast and newsletter Your Turn with Allison Aubrey, NPR's Allison Aubrey went in search of tools to help navigate midlife — starting with this survey to rank one's character strengths.
articles.title: Hit a midlife wall? This test identifies your strengths and what matters to you

articles.author: Eric McDaniel
articles.description: The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are looking into the mailings, some of which included an unidentified powdery white substance.
articles.title: Suspicious mailings to election officials, congressional offices under investigation

articles.author: Rachel Treisman
articles.description: Congress and a federal agency are threatening to weaken the country's historic preservation law, fueling a backlash that critics say is as fiery as the one that led to the law's creation 60 years ago.
articles.title: U.S. historic preservation law faces the most serious threat in its 60-year history

articles.author: Jennifer Teresa Villanueva
articles.description: For eight years, photographer Jennifer Teresa Villanueva has documented her Mexican American family's everyday life in Chicago, capturing intimate moments of love, labor and sacrifice.
articles.title: Inside a Chicago home, a photographer documents the life her family built

articles.author: Julie Appleby
articles.description: The Trump administration provided few details about its process for canceling hundreds of thousands of Affordable Care Act enrollments — even as the next stage of the anti-fraud effort is underway.
articles.title: After booting 760K off ACA health plans, the Trump administration adds some people back

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: Ukrainian drones attacked a refinery in Russia's Ryazan region early Thursday, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that a brief truce spurned by Moscow was over.
articles.title: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian oil refineries, officials say, after brief truce

articles.author: Eyder Peralta
articles.description: One plays the bull, the other the bullfighter, as a pair practices a dance of death in a sport that's prohibited in the Mexican capital city.
articles.title: Greetings from Mexico City, where a bullfighting ban doesn't stop this matador training

articles.author: Andee Tagle
articles.description: Cold and flu season is here. Before someone in your household gets hit, make sure you have these essential meds and comfort items in your medicine cabinet.
articles.title: Make a 'sick day' kit for cold and flu season before your household gets hit

articles.author: Ashley Lopez
articles.description: Some key voters in Georgia say deep frustration and disappointment with President Trump are motivating their election plans just weeks before Election Day.
articles.title: These swing voters regret voting for Trump and it's influencing their midterm choices

articles.author: Ben Doherty
articles.description:
Widespread manhunt in Dulwich Hill after man reportedly seen carrying longarm weapon

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A large swathe of Dulwich Hill in Sydney’s inner west has been locked down by police as they search for a man reportedly carrying a shotgun who allegedly set alight a stolen car in the area before fleeing on foot.
A police helicopter and armed tactical police focused their search for the man on an area around Williams Parade and Constitution Road.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sydney suburb in lockdown as police search for man seen with shotgun

articles.author: Penry Buckley
articles.description:
Jeff Bacon, managing director of Oceania Precision, has been described by the NSW party’s leader as ‘my go-to man on the firearms industry’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A firearms manufacturer hoping to represent One Nation in New South Wales wants to repeal gun laws introduced following the Bondi beach massacre, after arguing “every single one” of the rifles he produces was banned in the state.
Earlier this month, One Nation’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, and the federal MP Barnaby Joyce revealed Jeff Bacon would be second on the party’s upper house ticket in the March state election.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Firearms manufacturer standing for One Nation in NSW opposes post-Bondi gun laws that ban his rifles

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Gabrielle Canon, Shrai Popat, Lucy Campbell, Shannon Ho and Siraj Datoo
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Sign up for the Breaking News US email

The US government could spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on a media campaign in South Africa to figure out why more white Afrikaners are not applying to become refugees to the US, as Donald Trump had hoped.
State department officials, according to an August proposal seen by the Guardian, outlined a roughly $335,000 research and advertising effort after applications to the refugee program “trended lower than expected” since Afrikaners were allowed to apply directly online in November 2025. The document, written by the US mission in South Africa with a department research unit for the embassy in Pretoria, admits officials know little about why.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pentagon says Trump and Hegseth ‘completely aligned’ on decision to cancel livestream of firing squad execution – as it happened

articles.author: Gabrielle Canon in Oakland
articles.description:
Largest blaze the Henderson fire near San Diego as strong winds and severe heat could fuel rapid spread
Multiple wildfires ignited across California on Thursday as the state braced for more strong winds and high temperatures that could fuel rapid fire growth over the next several days.
The largest blaze, dubbed the Henderson fire, erupted in Camp Pendleton, a San Diego Marine Corps training base, and quickly consumed more than 1,000 acres. Evacuations have been issued and officials briefly closed part of the Interstate 5, a major highway in the region.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Evacuations issued as multiple wildfires ignite in hot, windy California

articles.author: Ariana Baio and agencies
articles.description:
Election officers in Louisiana and Oklahoma receive a powdery substance, prompting evacuations
The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service are investigating letters sent to state officials and election offices across the country containing an “unknown substance”.
Just weeks before November’s US midterm elections, election officers in Louisiana and Oklahoma received envelopes containing a powdery substance, leading to evacuations. A similar package containing white powder was also sent to the Ohio secretary of state, but the US Postal Service intercepted the package.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: FBI investigates letters with ‘unknown substance’ sent to US election officials

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
articles.description:
Two people critical in hospital as officials in Bend say 16-year-old suspect shot dead by bystander

Oregon elementary school shooting: what we know so far

A 16-year-old shooter opened fire at an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, killing three children and a teacher before he was shot dead by a community member, authorities said at an evening news conference.
The dead children at Silver Rail elementary school were aged five, eight and 11, officials said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Shooter kills three children and one teacher at Oregon elementary school

articles.author: Gabrielle Canon
articles.description:
The remains of Edward Lelburian Jackson were first discovered in 2022, and an initial autopsy revealed he was killed decades ago
After four years, a piece of the haunting mystery uncovered in the waning waters of drought-stricken Lake Mead has been solved.
Since the remains of an unknown homicide victim were discovered stuffed inside a barrel in 2022, Las Vegas investigators have been searching not for his killer – but for his identity. At a press conference on Thursday, Clark county coroner Melanie Rouse shared his name publicly for the first time: Edward Lelburian Jackson.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Police reveal identity of man found in a barrel in drought-stricken Lake Mead

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
Attack was the first on Aden’s Al-Maashiq palace ⁠in the latest fighting between ​the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia
Yemen’s Houthis fired missiles at the presidential palace complex in the southern city of Aden on Thursday, killing five people, the government said, as the Saudi-led coalition listed dozens of Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure in ⁠recent weeks.
The attack was the first on Aden’s Al-Maashiq palace ⁠in the current conflict between ​the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The palace is the seat of Yemen’s Saudi-backed and internationally recognised government.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Houthi missiles strike Yemen presidential palace, killing five

articles.author: Andrew Roth in Kyiv
articles.description:
Moscow sends swarms of drones to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine as Zelenskyy says Kyiv will restart strikes on Russian oil refineries
The White House’s unilateral effort to negotiate an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine has collapsed as Moscow sent a record swarm of drones overnight to attack infrastructure in central Ukraine and Kyiv appeared to resume strikes on Russian oil refineries despite warnings from Donald Trump.
Moscow accused Ukraine of launching a strike against a Russian oil refinery in the Ryazan region, its first since Trump abruptly declared an “energy ceasefire” that neither Russia nor Ukraine said they had agreed to.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes as Trump ‘energy ceasefire’ collapses

articles.author: Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor
articles.description:
UK defence secretary says he has been ‘reassured directly’ counterpart Pete Hegseth that Starlink system has been restored as he seeks to cool tensions
Wes Streeting urged the US to stand by Ukraine on his visit to the American capital and sought to cool tensions between the two countries in the wake of the Starlink row that is threatening to set back Kyiv’s war effort.
The British defence secretary, giving a speech before a meeting with his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, argued that supporting Ukraine was in the long-term interests of Washington, and a business opportunity.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Wes Streeting urges US to back Ukraine on Washington visit after Starlink row

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah  and agencies
articles.description:
Two people critically hurt when vehicle carrying HGV drivers hit stationary train in Calais, say French authorities
Nineteen people have been injured after a minibus collided with a stationary freight train at the loading platform of the Eurotunnel near Calais, French authorities have said.
Pas-de-Calais underprefect Agathe Cury said 18 passengers and the bus driver were injured in the incident.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nineteen injured in collision between minibus and train on Eurotunnel loading platform

articles.author: Ben Quinn Political correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: ITV investigation shows leader stood by mayoral candidate who said Labour MP should ‘go home to the Caribbean’
Nigel Farage was told by a senior Reform official that he was “protecting” a high-profile mayoral candidate accused of making racist comments about David Lammy, an undercover investigation has revealed.
The latest footage from an undercover investigation by ITV also shows Sarah Pochin, one of two female MPs for Reform, complaining that other party officials “are so fucking chauvinistic” and that “they just exclude you if you are a woman”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Farage accused of ‘protecting’ Reform candidate over racist slurs against David Lammy

articles.author: Emine Sinmaz
articles.description:
Woman claims comedian ‘pranced around like an ostrich’ before forcing himself on her in hotel room attack
Russell Brand transformed into a “monster” when he allegedly made a woman take half-naked photographs of him before raping her in a hotel room at a Labour party conference, a court has heard.
The 51-year-old comedian has denied attacking the woman, who broke down in tears in the witness box at Southwark crown court as she told how she could not fight him off.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russell Brand made alleged rape victim take photos of him half naked, trial told

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
Experts say seeking alternatives that deliver the same dose of oestrogen by the same method is key
Women in the UK are again facing shortages of some HRT products, with warnings they could persist for weeks. We take a look at the situation.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK HRT shortages: which products are affected and what to do about it

articles.author: Helena Smith
articles.description:
Demonstrators demand resignation of Edi Rama after three days of clashes in capital Tirana
Albania’s prime minister has said he will not resign as a protest movement, initially prompted by a proposal to build a Trump family-backed resort in the Balkan state, turned violent with clashes convulsing the capital for a third consecutive day.
Speaking on Thursday after calls by students who this week assumed control of the anti-government demonstrations that have rattled Tirana since June, Edi Rama said: “Governments are changed through democratic elections. We had elections last year, not a revolution.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Albania’s prime minister vows not to resign over student-led protests

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Nato source says drones came from Russia, while Romania’s president says attacking commercial ships ‘is unacceptable and has to stop’
Seven sailors are missing after drones struck two tankers near Romania’s Black Sea ⁠coast, setting them ablaze and raising ⁠fresh security concerns on a ​vital shipping route used by Ukraine.
A Nato military source told Reuters the drones that had hit the Wine Trader and the Yara J came from Russia. “The drones that caused ⁠the fires on board two tankers inside Romanian territorial waters were of Russian origin,” the source said.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Seven sailors missing after drones strike tankers near Romania’s Black Sea coast

articles.author: Jasper Jolly
articles.description:
Water company tells creditors it will not survive long enough to agree refinancing deal without more money
Thames Water has asked its creditors for another £2.4bn as the embattled water company comes close to running out of cash.
The UK’s largest water company said on Thursday it needed another short-term cash injection because it would be unable to reach a longer-term deal to sort out its giant debt pile before running out of cash by “the end of 2026 or the start of 2027”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Thames Water asks for £2.4bn more to avoid going bust this year or early 2027

articles.author: Rajeev Syal and Diane Taylor
articles.description:
Home secretary says she will block all Eritreans from UK unless a returns deal is agreed for rejected asylum seekers and criminals
Shabana Mahmood has been accused of launching a “perfunctory political gimmick” by the Eritrean government in a row over the return of rejected asylum seekers and criminals.
After the home secretary threatened to block all Eritreans from entering the UK unless a returns deal was agreed, the country’s embassy claimed the UK had failed to engage in “meaningful and appropriate” dialogue.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Eritrea accuses Shabana Mahmood of ‘political gimmick’ over visa ban threat

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Rewritten indictment accuses ex-Venezuela president and wife Cilia Flores of leading campaign of torture
Nicolás Maduro insisted on Thursday during an appearance in a New York court that torture allegations in a rewritten drug trafficking indictment against the deposed Venezuelan president and his wife were “false accusations”.
Maduro, shackled at the ankles, was brought to court to face the new charges accusing the couple of leading a state-sponsored campaign of repression that tortured scores of victims, including three Americans.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nicolás Maduro tells New York court new torture allegations are ‘false’

articles.author: Daniel Boffey in Port Stanley, Falkland Islands
articles.description:
Santiago Caputo cites election of Sagal Abdi-Wali as MP and calls UK a threat to the west in post shared by Argentina’s president
The chief adviser to Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has cited the election of Sagal Abdi-Wali to the UK parliament as evidence of the Islamisation of Britain and further reason for Argentina to take sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.
In a post on social media, Santiago Caputo, who is reportedly taking a key role in Argentina’s strategy over the Falklands, suggested that the taking of the south Atlantic islands was necessary to prevent the “interference of an Islamic state” in the region.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Milei adviser claims UK being ‘colonised by Islam’ as Falklands row grows

articles.author: Kalyeena Makortoff
articles.description:
Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets

Business news – live updates

Larry Elliott: the global economy is muddling through. But a storm is coming

An accelerating sell-off of AI-linked shares has hit global markets, as fears over rising inflation and future interest rate hikes spooked traders already wary of the heavily indebted sector.
South Korea’s benchmark Kospi 200 index, which is heavily skewed towards the companies that make memory chips, fell more than 8% overnight to a six-month closing low, triggering circuit breakers that brought trading to a halt at various points.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt

articles.author: Adam Morton and Sarah Basford Canales
articles.description:
Madeleine King told press club emissions from NT fossil fuel basin ‘are accounted for and offset’ but research found 95% of emissions this decade would not have to be offset

Sign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter here

The resources minister, Madeleine King, is facing calls to correct her claim in a major speech that all greenhouse gas emissions from developing a massive fossil fuel basin in the Northern Territory will be offset to limit their impact on the climate.
Speaking at the National Press Club in Canberra on Wednesday, King defended her support for the development of the Beetaloo gas basin south of Darwin after being asked if she was comfortable with the impact that the emissions from the gas would have on Australians.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Resources minister faces calls to correct her claim all Beetaloo emissions will be offset

articles.author: Ben Smee
articles.description:
The controversial legislation may end up placing large sections of its suburban support – critical to the party’s lead in the polls – on the bonfire

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

For almost two years, the Liberal National party’s strategy for government in Queensland has been to stay well clear of issues that risk burning through political capital.
On Wednesday, one of the most tentative conservative governments in recent history announced plans for sweeping and controversial changes to workplace laws.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Queensland’s LNP has trodden softly in government. It’s now baring its teeth over the power to break up workers’ strikes

articles.author: Reuters in Islamabad
articles.description:
Another three pupils from al-Khair school in Peshawar in critical condition after search for survivors
At least 34 schoolchildren and a female teacher have died after the roof of a school collapsed during morning classes in the northern Pakistani city ⁠of Peshawar.
As panicked parents ​and relatives thronged the site of the privately run al-Khair school to search for their loved ones, rescue workers spent hours pulling children from the rubble.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pakistan school roof collapse kills at least 34 children and teacher

articles.author: Sarah Johnson
articles.description:
At least 320 people detained for ‘acts against nature’ after law criminalising homosexuality toughened, HRW reports
Mass arrests, forced HIV testing and barriers to legal representation are part of an escalating crackdown against LGBTQ+ people in Senegal, according to a new report.
More than 320 individuals have been arrested and detained on allegations of “acts against nature” since February, according to HIV Justice Network, an organisation quoted in the Human Rights Watch (HRW) report. Among these, at least 84 were charged with “voluntary HIV transmission”, solely on the basis of their HIV status.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: LGBTQ+ people go into hiding in Senegal as hundreds are arrested

articles.author: Australian Associated Press
articles.description:
Western Australian police say woman ‘experienced numbness to her tongue’ after tasting the curry at her workplace in Perth

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A woman has been charged after allegedly poisoning a co-worker’s lunch curry with snail pellets.
Western Australian police say a 58-year-old woman brought a container of curry to share with colleagues at her workplace in Perth’s southern suburbs in February.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Woman charged after allegedly poisoning colleague’s curry lunch with snail pellets

articles.author: Kate Lamb and agencies
articles.description:
Having tried cloud seeding and water bombing, one pilot project will see dry ice dispersed by plane across the province of South Sumatra
As fires ravage Indonesia, emitting a toxic smoke that has drawn the ire of regional neighbours, the government is testing an unusual new approach to tackle the haze: dry ice.
Having tried cloud seeding, water bombing and sending in army personnel to fight the fires, Indonesia’s coordinating security minister said dry ice would be dropped on the province of South Sumatra on Thursday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Indonesia fights fire with dry ice as toxic haze spreads across region

articles.author: Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
articles.description:
Congress approves constitutional amendment that bans six-day workweeks, which could affect up to 30 million
Brazil’s congress has approved a constitutional amendment to shorten the working week to a maximum of 40 hours, a move that could affect 30 million workers and that will hand a political victory to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ahead of the presidential runoff in under two weeks.
In an attempt to overturn the first-round lead secured by his opponent, far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula has strongly championed the amendment, which will give some workers an extra day off each week.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Brazil cuts work week to 40 hours in win for Lula ahead of runoff

articles.author: Aram Roston in Washington
articles.description:
Exclusive: Israel has not permitted US-led project to house 150 international troops to move forward
Israel is refusing to allow a key military outpost project for Donald Trump’s Board of Peace to proceed in Gaza, the Guardian has learned.
In early August, the Board of Peace, the international organization authorized in 2025 by the UN and chaired by the US president, issued its first construction contract for Gaza: Louisiana-based Arkel International would construct a military outpost for 150 international troops that would be the vanguard of an international stabilization force.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israel blocks construction of key Gaza base created by Trump peace board

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers
The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Hannah Ellis-Petersen; produced by Angus Neale; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin; executive producer Zoe Hitch
articles.description:
A fresh wave of protests by India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has been met with a brutal crackdown by Narendra Modi’s government and the closure of a historic protest site in Delhi. Two of the movement’s leaders have been imprisoned for five days for violating suppression measures. The protests, which began over frustration about education and unemployment, are now focused on voting rights. Modi’s government denies claims it is seeking to disenfranchise millions of voters. But its treatment of protesters has been criticised by the UN and Amnesty International and raised concerns that India is sliding further into autocracy. Lucy Hough speaks to South Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen – watch on YouTube
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India’s cockroach protesters defy Modi’s crackdown – The Latest

articles.author: Peter Beaumont Senior international correspondent
articles.description:
Vessels were hit by missiles as rise in strikes suggests Iran is trying to close waterway before US midterm elections
Two container ships near the strait of Hormuz have ⁠sunk after being struck by missiles, amid the sharpest rise in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran.
The increase in attacks suggests Iran is trying to fully close the strategic waterway in an attempt to frustrate Donald Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Two container ships sink near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacks

articles.author: Rebecca Bailey China correspondent
articles.description:
International alliance of China-sceptic legislators warns of risks inherent in misjudging bilateral relationship
The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship.
An audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by lack of expertise, report says

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Global human rights commitments adopted by government extend reach to enablers of unlawful activity
The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners.
The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements

articles.author: Melody Schreiber
articles.description:
Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr
Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.
The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns

articles.author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
articles.description:
Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posts footage of citizenship ceremony to Instagram
Joni Mitchell has become a US citizen, after first moving to the country in the mid-1960s. The Canada-born singer-songwriter, 82, posted footage of her citizenship ceremony on her Instagram account, along with a photo of her next to an American flag, accompanied by the caption: “A journey that began 62 years ago.”
It means that Mitchell can now vote in US elections, something that she had complained she wasn’t able to do.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Joni Mitchell becomes US citizen: ‘A journey that began 62 years ago’

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das will spend spend five days in prison for entering Delhi’s Jantar Mantar – a historic protest site that has been closed by authorities

Why Indian voters are on the streets

Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.
A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Leaders of India’s Cockroach party jailed for violating ban on protest site

articles.author: Deepa Parent
articles.description:
Rights groups warn of Tehran regime’s increasing use of executions to suppress dissent, with at least 600 this year
Human rights groups have raised the alarm over the growing number of death sentences and executions in Iran, after reports that a 23-year-old woman, Najmeh Amini, has been sentenced to death for blasphemy over a social-media post.
Amini, an accounting student, is being held in Vakilabad prison in the north-east city of Mashhad. She has been sentenced to more than 12 years in prison and death in separate cases heard by a revolutionary and a criminal court.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Iranian woman handed death sentence for ‘blasphemy’ in social media post

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Shaikh Azizur Rahman
articles.description:
Anger at electoral roll changes has boiled over, sparking a crisis for Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist government

Leaders of India’s Cockroach party jailed

Born into a small village in West Bengal, Shahida Fakir had always taken her vote for granted. That was, until it was suddenly taken away. She presented officials with her Indian birth certificate and family land documents from the village going back to 1962.
Both her parents had been on the electoral roll going back decades, so she showed proof of that too. But when the final revised voter list came out in April, Fakir was not on it.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘How do you explain the deletion of 130 million names?’: why Indian voters are on the streets

articles.author: Justin McCurry in Tokyo
articles.description:
FSB security agency said reporter was arrested on island of Sakhalin, alleging he was collecting information about Russia’s defences
Russia has arrested a Japanese journalist on the far east island of Sakhalin and accused him of spying, in the latest sign of rising tensions between Moscow and Tokyo.
Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova identified the reporter as Yuki Imai, from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, adding that he had been accused of “conducting espionage activities on Russian territory”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on allegations of spying

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Microbiologist Aili Wang, 32, poisoned tea of colleague in Wyoming who had pending patents, prosecutors allege
A Wyoming microbiology graduate student from China has been arrested on accusations she poisoned the tea of a colleague who had pending patents and with whom she did not get along, then tried to flee the country after police questioned her.
Aili Wang, 32, was arrested 6 October at Los Angeles international airport, where prosecutors allege she sought to return to China. With her were laptops, electronic storage devices and documents now in the possession of police, who allege Wang was seen on surveillance video rummaging through the desk of the victim who specialized in technology for disease treatment – research similar to work she had done in China.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Graduate student accused of poisoning colleague and trying to flee to China arrested at LAX

articles.author: Dani Anguiano and Gabrielle Canon
articles.description:
Boardwalk destroyed in Long Beach and homes damaged, while Baja California in Mexico and Las Vegas also affected
Southern California coastal communities are picking up the pieces after a weekend of extreme weather brought flooding that overtook city streets and intense waves battered beachside homes.
The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel hit Mexico’s Baja California over the weekend as well as southern California and Las Vegas. While meteorologists noted that Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it approached California, it still left a trail of destruction.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Intense waves and floods batter California waterfront homes and boardwalks

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
Marches in Delhi against changes to voting registration led to dragnets, internet blackouts – and questions about India’s electoral independence. Plus, the cinematographer capturing the beauty of the mundane
• Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.
Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Shock, anger and a crackdown: why a contentious electoral revision has sparked outrage

articles.author: Melody Schreiber
articles.description:
Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.
This article was amended on 13 October 2026. A previous version said CIDRAP first reported news that the research trial was approved by the Denmark ethics committee. Rolling Stone had actually reported the news first.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau

When Donald Trump pledged to end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours of re-entering the White House last year, no one with any depth of insight into the conflict believed him. But Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image as a master dealmaker. After a period when it seemed that Kyiv’s European allies had steered the US president away from pro‑Kremlin partisanship, he has reverted to the grotesque view that Ukrainian capitulation is a necessary precondition for peace.
These are the perilous circumstances in which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham on Wednesday in Downing Street. In recent days, the US president has called for a change of government in Ukraine. He claimed that a partial ceasefire had been agreed, while Russia escalated its bombardments. According to Mr Zelenskyy, the latest missile strikes have come without the intelligence warnings from the US that have, in the past, facilitated self-defence. There have been reports of Ukrainian soldiers losing access to the Starlink satellite network, controlled by Elon Musk, the US tech oligarch. This raises suspicion of coordinated pressure to tip the scales in Russia’s favour after many months when Mr Putin’s forces have failed to deliver significant advances and his country’s economy has been suffering from the effect of Ukrainian missile and drone counterstrikes.

You still risk getting arrested by immigration agents and thrown into a detention centre, but never mind that! Instead, luxuriate in the fact that none of the poorly paid Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff with whom you interact will be sitting down. The government recently got rid of all the chairs at travel document checking stations, arguing that “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism” and strengthens “our security posture and … commitment to hospitality”. Funnily enough, border patrol and customs officers have not adopted the same policy. Perhaps because their job tends to involve being as inhospitable as possible.
TSA agents aren’t the only US workers getting sore calf muscles during their shifts. Unlike their European and British counterparts, cashiers at US supermarkets have traditionally been forced to stand while working. The US’s upright obsession seems to be down to a Protestant work ethic and a lack of labour laws. Sitting apparently conveys laziness to the discerning American consumer. Over the years there have been numerous right-to-sit lawsuits pushing back on mandatory standing but, while things are shifting slightly, seated supermarket cashiers are still unusual. One exception is Aldi, which has been expanding aggressively in the US. Cashiers get chairs at Aldi because (surprise) it’s more efficient when your workers’ feet aren’t aching all the time.

A cast member of The Archers has said its actors have been angered by the BBC’s decision to axe the show’s new studio, in a move that could lead to it being recorded away from its home in Birmingham.
Ben Norris, who plays Ben Archer in the world’s longest-running soap opera, said the decision risked having a real impact on the quality of the show and placing an “extraordinary burden” on its crew.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Archers cast ‘angry’ at BBC decision to scrap new Birmingham studio

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Government says ambition for 2036 will be good for food and climate resilience, but concerns remain over funding
The government has set an ambition to increase the share of English land farmed organically to 10% by 2036, but concerns remain over how the transition will be funded.
Currently, just 3.4% of England’s agricultural land is farmed organically, one of the smallest shares in Europe. France, for example, farms 10.4% of its land organically, and aims to increase this to 18% by 2027.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Plan unveiled to increase share of land farmed organically in England to 10%

articles.description:
Jason O’Connell is suspected of having used smart glasses that turned his lenses into tiny teleprompters. Periodic flashing in his spectacles could be seen as the Senedd member for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr spoke for five minutes without a glance at his notes on 30 September. In the following days, other Welsh assembly members said the issue of smart glasses – popularised by Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta – needed to be dealt with at pace, with explicit guidance about their use developed. There is no suggestion O’Connell's glasses were recording
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Reform UK politician appears to use smart glasses as teleprompter during Senedd debate – video

articles.author: Mark Brown North of England correspondent
articles.description:
Relatives of William Chapman say footage of attack shared online ‘deeply offensive’ and causing them ‘severe distress’
The family of a man killed by a tiger at a wildlife park in the UK have spoken about their “severe distress” at the circulation of online media after Donald Trump reposted a video of the incident.
William Chapman, 23, was mauled to death after entering an enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, on Saturday.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Family of man killed by tiger criticise online content after Trump reposts video

articles.author: Steven Morris
articles.description:
Engineer Tristan Ralph describes task of maintaining and running Bristol structure without public money
The job does not give the holder age-old perks such as the right to drive sheep across the great structure, but the title “bridge master” does have a certain ring to it.
“I don’t tend to say I’m the bridge master when I’m at a party,” said Tristan Ralph, the current holder of the title. “But people do seem to know and bring it up. It’s a job less ordinary, isn’t it? It’s a Victorian sounding title and people are really, really interested.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘A big responsibility’: Clifton Suspension Bridge master hails £7.6m renovation

articles.author: Hannah Al-Othman North of England correspondent
articles.description:
Rapper to visit Lincolnshire town 16 years after saying he had never been there in his hit Pass Out
The rapper Tinie Tempah has said he will finally visit Scunthorpe – 16 years after he announced to the world that he had never been to the town in his number one hit Pass Out.
His decision follows a campaign by fans, led by Ben Johns, a Scunthorpe resident, who carried a cardboard cutout of the artist around the Lincolnshire town and encouraged people to pre-save Tempah’s new album.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tinie Tempah says he will finally visit Scunthorpe after campaign by fans

articles.author: Zoe Wood
articles.description:
Declining stocks and increased fishing pressure have led to lower sustainability ratings for two popular cod alternatives
UK shoppers have previously been urged to avoid UK-caught cod and to buy European hake or coley instead – but now these fish are in trouble, too.
The Marine Conservation Society (MCS), an environmental charity, publishes its Good Fish Guide to help consumers and businesses make sustainable seafood choices. It uses a traffic-light system to rate seafood according to the health of fish stocks and environmental impact.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Scale back on hake and coley, seafood charity tells shoppers

articles.author: Patrick Barkham
articles.description:
Citizen scientists on UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme recorded insect visits to flowers during 10-minute surveys
Ubiquitous urban plants often derided as “weeds” are the most attractive to pollinating insects.
The autumn blooms of common ivy, rich in pollen and nectar, are the most visited by insects including bees and butterflies, according to an eight-year study.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pollinating insects flock to plants gardeners might think of as ‘weeds’

articles.author: Aamna Mohdin Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Investigation finds racial inequality in live music industry rife and many genres labelled ‘high risk’ despite lack of evidence 
Black and south Asian music events in London face disproportionate cancellations, restrictions and licensing barriers compared with white events, according to a two-year investigation into racial inequality in the capital’s live music industry.
The Race Equality in Music Event Licensing (REMEL) report, led by Black Lives in Music, estimates that cancellations, displacement and events prevented from taking place cost London £127m to £141m annually, with projected losses exceeding £650m over five years.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Barriers facing black and south Asian music events ‘cost London up to £141m a year’

articles.author: Anna Bawden
articles.description:
Research shows that the best linguists process unfamiliar foreign speech sounds more like non-speech sounds
If you want to get really good at French, Arabic or Hungarian, don’t start with rote learning vocabulary and grammar, focus on how they sound instead, research suggests.
A new study of how humans learn modern languages has found that the brains of the most talented linguists hear foreign terms as random noise, not words.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Stop making sense: focus on sounds to help learn a language, study suggests

articles.author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Conference to explore legacy of Naseem Khan’s seminal 1976 report about  exclusion of minority ethnic artists
It is 50 years since cultural historian Naseem Khan’s challenge to the British arts establishment was first published, and the question of who and what counts as British continues to be contested.
The Arts Britain Ignores – Khan’s groundbreaking 1976 report, commissioned by organisations including the then Arts Council of Great Britain, presented a vision of a pluralistic national culture, in which the creativity of Britons of diverse ethnic backgrounds – from bhangra music, to black painters and Ukrainian dance – should be recognised, supported and respected.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: 50 years on from Arts Britain Ignores: how much has changed for black and Asian artists?

articles.author: Andrew Gregory Health editor
articles.description:
Cambridge University study suggests stark gender divide in misdiagnosis, with women also waiting longer for treatment
Women with autoimmune conditions are up to 74% more likely than men to be told their symptoms are psychological or psychosomatic, and face much longer waits for a diagnosis and treatment, a study suggests.
Hundreds of millions of people – about one in 10 globally – are affected by autoimmune conditions, which can cause a range of health issues including fatigue, muscle pain and rashes.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Women ‘more likely to be told autoimmune conditions are psychological’

articles.author: Dalya Alberge
articles.description:
Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality
Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore.
Now fourth-century coins, among other finds at a newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, suggest the medieval tale was rooted in reality, to the excitement of archaeologists.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real

articles.author: Diane Taylor
articles.description:
As ‘one in, one out’ scheme ends, refugees still want to cross the Channel despite French police aggression and hostile welcomes
The smuggler works quickly. Using a small shovel, he digs up a dinghy buried in a sand dune on a beach not far from Boulogne-sur-Mer, assembles it and affixes a motor in record time.
“I never saw anyone work like this,” says Amad, from Iraq, one of a group of about 30 asylum seekers waiting to cross the Channel. “The UK government wants to stop the smugglers, but they are smart. They have plan A, plan B and plan C, so there is always a way for them to get people across this sea. For as long as asylum seekers will pay them, there is too much money involved for them to give up.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Is there a different way to fix the small boats crisis?

articles.author: Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty with Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor; produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke Smith; executive producers Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale
articles.description:
Are we really living through ‘end-times fascism’? Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor think so.
In a new series from the Guardian, the pair speak to Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty in an extended interview. From Trump 2.0 and the rise of the tech billionaires to Gaza and the climate emergency, Klein and Taylor argue we are not just lurching from crisis to crisis but are in a new and dangerous moment in history. But they haven’t given up hope of a fightback
You can watch the full interview with Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor here.
Aditya’s suggested reading:
Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s End Times Fascism is out now and available here. It began life as a special essay in the Guardian, which you can read here.
A different take on whether Trump 2.0 is fascist comes from the economist Branko Milanović on his brilliant Substack.
Elon Musk gives Donald Trump millions, and Trump gives Musk vast access to power. To read more, look at Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff’s long read for the Guardian and their recent book Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed.
For some phenomenal reporting on Trump’s second term, look at Regime Change by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan.
How did the business class learn to love Trump and embrace chaos? Paul Heideman gives a lucid analysis in his recent book Rogue Elephant.
Klein and Taylor’s book regularly cites Karen Hao’s Empire of AI.
There’s also The Nerd Reich, just out from Gil Durán.
If you enjoyed Yanis Varoufakis in our last episode of Radical Thinking, check out his book Technofeudalism.
As for how AI is imposing a new age of total corporate control, The Rulers by Cecilia Rikap is a must.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Gaza is a moral tear in the universe’: Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty – podcast

Labour fends off Green party to win Holborn and St Pancras byelection

articles.author: Esther Addley
articles.description:
Inquest hears details of how three women spent their final days but why they ended their lives may never be known
Jane Adetoro and her younger sisters, Christina and Rebecca Walters, were “the closest sisters and the best friends”, according to their family. Devoted to their father, Joseph, whom they messaged every day, the adult siblings lived quiet lives in the flat they shared in west London and would do everything together.
When they died in May this year, it was no different. Early in the morning of 13 May, the sisters’ bodies were recovered from the sea in Brighton, hours after a taxi had dropped the three women at the beachfront.

articles.title: A lake pilgrimage and a quiet car ride to the beach: last hours of sisters who took own lives in Brighton

articles.author: Ben Quinn with photographs by Graeme Robertson
articles.description:
Little if any sign Bury Park is a place where any group might fear to tread, despite Tory MP’s comments to the contrary
From behind the counter of his chippie, Tanner Ahmed is wrestling with the notion that the regular stop-off point for fans attending Luton Town’s nearby football ground could be in a “no-go zone” for white people.
“The whole point of setting up was to cater for thousands who were coming through here every week, especially in the first year when the club was in the Premier League,” said Ahmed, affectionately known as Mr T, in the Bury Park area, a predominantly Asian district of Luton.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘I feel perfectly safe’: white Lutonians on the town’s supposed no-go zones

articles.author: Ian Sample Science editor
articles.description:
International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of years
After decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour.
Delegates from 69 countries cast their votes on Thursday at a conference in France of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which ensures the world sticks to the same standards of time, weight, distance and more.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour

Chip makers and tech investors such as Samsung and SoftBank plunge as potential interest rate hikes spook markets

Business news – live updates

articles.title: Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debt

articles.author: Aisha Down
articles.description:
Discover-Tech’s Controlium software lets clients mass-profile internet users then covertly hack targets, say researchers at University of Toronto
An Israeli advertising agency has been serving millions of online adverts that allow “zero-click” spyware to be used against targets, researchers at a Canadian university have said.
Citizen Lab, a digital investigations research unit at the University of Toronto, said it believed dozens of devices at the Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera had been compromised by spyware delivered through ads run by Discover-Tech, which describes itself as a specialised digital advertising agency.

articles.author: Tom Regan
articles.description:
The studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series
Where do you go after Mario? It’s a question the team at Ubisoft Paris found itself pondering three years ago after wrapping up work on the charming turn-based tactics adventure, Mario + Rabbids: Sparks of Hope, sequel to its unexpected crossover hit, Mario + Rabbids: Kingdom Battle. By melding a rather specialist genre with video gaming’s biggest household name, the developer introduced chin-stroking strategic play to a whole new audience. “Having the opportunity to work with the Mario franchise was a privilege, and it’s still something I’m very proud of,” says level designer director, Julien Vial. “I still remember seeing the first prototype and being blown away by all the possibilities.”
Now, Ubisoft Paris has returned with a new project, but this time the studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series Rainbow Six. Where Mario and Rabbids saw squishy creatures bounce harmlessly across levels as Mario encased foes in honey, Rainbow Six Tactics, a turn-based tactical spin-off from Rainbow Six Siege, sees balaclava-clad insurgents take shrapnel rounds to the chest. A seamless tonal shift, then.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics

In the final part of our series on the country, Poles tell how wages have soared – along with the cost of living

Will military spending help or hinder Poland’s growth story?

Poland’s push for EU energy resilience amid Russian aggression

For some, the Soviet-era Palace of Culture and Science is a drunk confectioner’s nightmare; standing as a relic of oppression that should have been demolished. For others, it is an icon on the skyline and a monumental warning from history.

US states sue ChatGPT maker and seek to force the company to change how its products work for young users 
Eight US states sued OpenAI Wednesday, alleging the ChatGPT maker is harming children en masse.
Kansas, Arizona, Montana, Iowa and four others allege the company’s products carried out “willful, dangerous, reckless and unlawful conduct” by coaxing children into harming themselves.

Hours before Apple and the ChatGPT maker were due to face off in court, a new allegation delayed the showdown 
An ⁠OpenAI employee who left the ChatGPT maker for Apple sent more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal ⁠account and later ⁠made a presentation ​about the unreleased product to senior Apple leadership, a new filing in the lawsuit between OpenAI and Apple alleges.

articles.description:
Accounts for the Westminster-based company behind ChatGPT show that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares last year
OpenAI’s London staff each received £2,318,181 on average last year, as the ChatGPT-maker poured Premier League football salaries into its bid to dominate the global AI race.
Accounts for OpenAI UK Ltd, which is based in Westminster but is opening a new HQ in London’s King’s Cross area, showed that 110 staff shared £87m in salaries and £168m in shares in the company, which is aiming to list on the stock market at a valuation of about $1tn.

Article in Atlantic claims The Blue Fighter was artificially generated, days after it won Caine prize for African writers
The Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using AI to write a prize-winning short story after an article in the Atlantic said software had flagged it as almost completely AI-generated.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter was announced as the winner of the prestigious Caine prize for African writers on 6 October. Five days later, The Atlantic published an article by the author and journalist Vauhini Vara titled: “Yet Another Literary prize winner Seems to Be AI.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza denies using AI to write prize-winning story

Experts say the technology could help terrorists and nation states with production but that significant hurdles remain
In his annual speech on threats to the nation, Sir Ken McCallum, the head of the UK’s intelligence service, MI5, warned that AI had the potential to “change the stakes” on existing and even new bioweapons. Here we look at how AI might help in the development of bioweapons and the hurdles that remain.

Jason O’Connell’s suspected use of the specs to aid his speech in Senedd reignites debate over AI-enabled devices
It was a flowing speech packed full of precise statistics – but Jason O’Connell, a Reform UK Senedd member, was not quite the gifted orator he had first appeared. articles.author: Keith Stuart
articles.description:
After years of sprawling ‘forever’ games, players are rediscovering the pleasures of more focused experiences. Could a new wave of independent arcades bring back the social side of gaming?
• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
There’s an important semi-nostalgic movement happening in games, and I’m excited about where it’s heading. But I don’t want to get ahead of myself here.
Over the last five years, major publishers, obsessed with the success of “forever games” such as Fortnite, Minecraft and Roblox, have been throwing hundreds of millions of dollars into their own sprawling, endlessly updating, battle-pass-infested mega franchises – each designed to take all our time and money. The result has been astounding failures such as Concord, Mindseye and Tales of the Shire. Even the good games – Crimson Desert, Path of Exile 2, Blood of the Dawnwalker – are so bloated they have become the unyielding masters of our precious few hours of free time.

articles.author: Matthew Castle
articles.description:
The kingdom of Hyrule has been prettified, the soundtrack is newly orchestrated and our hero feels strikingly different under the thumbs … we play a hands-on demo of Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of a 1998 game-changer
When beloved art is revisited and revised, a familiar cry is often heard: “You’re ruining my childhood!” But with Nintendo’s Switch 2 remake of Ocarina of Time, there are also livelihoods at risk: specifically, the man running the shooting gallery in Castle Town. In the original 1998 version of the game, he’d rip off players as they funnelled rupees and fudged the then still novel analogue-stick aiming. But in 2026 we have more responsive frame rates and a motion-controlled slingshot that allows precision adjustments. His targets tumble on the first go, and with them his entire business model. Even in Hyrule, the death of the high street seems inevitable.
Bad news for him but great news for Link, a child of the forest who, as in 1998, steps into a vast fantasy kingdom to vanquish a great evil, but now does so with a number of improvements. The boy can now sprint, preventing the ignominy of endless roly-polies to zip across grassy plains. He has a manual jump, free-rotating camera, a scrolling inventory bar that replaces menu screen faff and, crucially, a fatter wallet for holding all those gems he fleeces from struggling shooting gallery owners. Yes, we are being asked to applaud features that have been the norm for decades elsewhere, but it’s undeniably striking to enter familiar territory with a hero who feels this different under the thumbs.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time preview – Link faces his scariest challenge yet: the 4K era

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
Pledge spanning five years from world’s most valuable firm comes as concerns about AI agents have risen

The $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmaker Nvidia is donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to support AI safety research.
The donation from the world’s most valuable company comes as the UK government confirmed its AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advance AI models, will be able to examine cutting-edge technology developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google before they are released.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nvidia, worth $5.5tn, donates $250m to UK for AI safety research

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan and Nick Robins-Early
articles.description:
From the FBI to local police departments, US authorities are increasingly warning of would-be terrorists using chatbots to plan attacks and anti-AI extremist threats 
In May 2025, a 25-year-old man detonated a car bomb outside a Palm Springs fertility clinic, killing himself and injuring four others. For many, it was a wake-up call about the threats to reproductive care facilities. For the FBI, though, it was also a sign of what the agency had feared for years: bad actors were using generative AI to plan and execute terror plots.
The suspect used an unnamed generative AI tool that failed to detect his request for bomb-making instructions, law enforcement officers wrote in a previously unreported document reviewed by the Guardian. The privacy of his conversation with the AI chatbot hindered alerting police that someone was looking up how to make a bomb, according to the memo.
How extremists could use AI to devise attacks and recruit new members
How AI could be used to disseminate and produce everything from deepfakes to election misinformation and child sexual abuse material (CSAM)
How people seeking information on how to make weaponry or bombs could use AI to circumvent police detection
How to ensure that officers could take advantage of AI tools in policing, for things like social media monitoring, while managing public concern over the use of these tools
Monitoring social media for opposition to AI and potential extremist attacks on datacenters
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tool and target: US law enforcement grapple with AI-enabled terrorism and anti-tech extremism

articles.description:
Congress calls for Match Group and others to do more to help victims like Mary, who lost $100,000 to app scammer
Mary met a man on the dating app Plenty of Fish in 2024. She told the Guardian she had been looking for a connection, but instead became the victim of a romance scam that cost her almost $100,000.
“There was a lot of conversation, and then it started with the constant contact, pressure and repeated asks for money,” Mary, who asked that her last name be withheld, said in an interview on Tuesday. “It just escalated really, really quickly.”

articles.title: ‘Like being in a vortex’: US report details extent of ‘devastating’ dating-app scams

articles.author: Taylor Telford
articles.description:
Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work
Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools.
Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported. While the US clings on to its status as the oldest constitutional democracy, the unholy alliance between the tech overlords and the White House is creating its own AI reality untethered to the will of the people.

The evidence seems to be everywhere. Each week headlines warn of teenagers addicted to phones, a loneliness epidemic and the dangers of AI. The release of The Social Reckoning leads us to ask, “How bad were those guys at Meta?” and then ultimately wonder, “How bad am I if I still use Instagram?” In our day-to-day, we observe workers eating lunch alone while scrolling and friends choosing online games over offline gatherings.

articles.description:
Evil Empire/Konami; PC, PS5, Switch, Xbox
There are buzzsaws and blood pits, bats burst into blood and demons burn to cinders. The series’ new emphasis on twitch-based action may annoy purists but you can’t call it dull

A gorgeously gothic Paris swarming with demons should be a perfect setting for Konami’s long-running vampiric adventure series. Unfortunately, while the sights and sounds of this vivid and haunting world leave a bold impression, developer Evil Empire doesn’t always provide an enjoyable experience to go with them. It takes far too long for the most imaginative elements of the game to be revealed.
Players take the role of Rose Belmont, daughter of vampire hunter (and Castlevania regular) Trevor Belmont and the witch Sypha Belnades, and her quest is to free Paris from demonic occupation. This murderous noctural journey feels best when you’re fighting monsters; combat is frenetic, sometimes to the point of being overwhelming, while boss fights require considerable focus and skill. Combat is the game’s strongest component and what sets it apart from previous entries. Minimising the series’ role-playing elements (levelling up has never felt more perfunctory) in favour of twitch-based action will annoy purists, but they’d be hard pressed to call battles dull.

This fetchingly presented horror game brings style and scares, but overextends itself with repetition
A small band of soldiers enters an abandoned facility, where puckered flesh sprouts from cold steel. It’s a promising but familiar start to a sci-fi horror story, with heavy overtones of Alien and The Thing. Neither of those, though, were so … dinky.
End of Abyss’s facility is presented as a kind of a model-village recreation of The Thing’s Outpost 31 that you peer into from above. Your little bobble-headed hero takes up a tiny fraction of the screen, with most of the remainder drenched in foggy darkness, or even blanked out entirely. This is a world of Usborne-style cutaways, where anything outside the walls is total blackness.
